narrative:
The model predicted an 82.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess long-term success, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your class ranking after the third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Standing in only the first decile, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model that you struggled to keep pace with your peers as the curriculum became more demanding. Your first-year ranking in the second decile reinforced this picture, though it carried less weight than the third-year result. These two early indicators of relative academic standing outweighed every other piece of information.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.60, compared with an average of 3.23 among accepted applicants, also nudged the prediction slightly higher, but its influence was noticeably smaller than your law-school deciles.

Taken together, the model saw a consistent pattern of lower-than-average performance in law school that it has learned strongly predicts difficulty passing the bar. To improve your chances in a future application, you should focus on raising your academic performance if you retake courses or enroll in a post-baccalaureate program, or consider gaining substantial work experience that demonstrates skills the model does not currently see in your record. Rebuilding a stronger academic trajectory is the clearest path to shifting this type of prediction.
